To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

brain networks involved motor control remain responsive, even after chronic spinal cord injury, and that these findings have implications for therapeutic strategies aimed at re-establishing spinal cord function.
the brain of people with SCI shows reorganization and preservation, which can be detected by functional neuroimaging techniques.

brain mapping studies during attempted and/or motor imagery tasks in people with SCI have identified the following patterns of reorganization of motor control: 1) increased activation, 2) decreased activation, 3) altered activation (shift in location), 4) preserved activation, 5) increased activation of subcortical structures, and 6) preserved activation of subcortex.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of brain function in patients with spinal cord injury (SCI).
the study of the reorganization of motor control in the brain of people with spinal cord injury (SCI), and how this reorganization is influenced by the level and severity of the injury.
the reorganization and the preservation of brain function after SCI, and how these processes can be influenced by rehabilitation interventions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the brain of people with SCI remains responsive and that the reorganization and/or preservation of motor control is a promising area for further study.

the brain is able to reorganize and preserve motor control of the spinal cord in people with SCI, and that this reorganization is influenced by the level and completeness of SCI, time after injury and extent of clinical recovery, as well as the type of motor task.
brain reorganization and preservation are important aspects of recovery of function following SCI.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are many different ways to approach brain mapping in people with SCI.
the reorganization and/or preservation of brain function after SCI may be a key to recovery of motor control.
the brain can reorganize itself to compensate for the loss of motor control after spinal cord injury.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain remains responsive to movement demands, even in chronic paralysis, and this responsiveness can be used to guide rehabilitation strategies.
the brain is plastic and can adapt to injury, and that the degree to which it adapts is related to the level and completeness of the injury.
brain mapping studies can reveal patterns of brain reorganisation in people with SCI.
